title: Contrast and concession: what the military said and what they did

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *sin embargo* and *no obstante* from B1 Unit 1, and *aunque* from A2 Unit 28. They set one fact against another. The history of the military governments is full of such contrasts: what the generals promised and what they did, or how one government differed from another.

sections.title: Three connectors
rows: however: starts a new sentence, comma after it
although: joins two clauses in one sentence

items.spanish: Los militares decían que querían defender el orden. Sin embargo, no devolvieron el poder pronto.
items.english: The military said they wanted to defend order. However, they did not give power back soon.

items.spanish: Aunque era un gobierno militar, su programa era de izquierda.
items.english: Although it was a military government, its programme was of the left.

items.spanish: En Perú el gobierno militar era de izquierda. No obstante, en Chile los militares combatieron a la izquierda.
items.english: In Peru the military government was of the left. Nevertheless, in Chile the military fought the left.

items.spanish: Algunos sectores apoyaron los golpes. Sin embargo, otros los rechazaron.
items.english: Some sectors supported the coups. However, others rejected them.

sections.content: Put a comma after *sin embargo* and *no obstante*. With *aunque* the clause comes first or second, and a comma separates them when *aunque* opens the sentence: *Aunque era un gobierno militar, …*.
